body: Could someone help me understand the remaining error I seem to be having the the automatic checks?

Thanks for the feedback and help so far guys (and I apologize for my ignorance. This really is my first time formally contributing to an open project like this). 

There are some remaining things I want to actually discuss regarding final implementation:

1. I chose to use the "alternate" convention for expressing the products of inertia in which the values are calculated as positive integrals and then negated when placed in the inertia tensor. I'm willing to be overruled here and, in fact, I'm beginning to question if I made the right decision. I'd like others' feedback here. 
2. For my application, I will likely be modifying the mass properties every time step as fuel is burned. It is inefficient to set the inertia vector, and then the products of inertia vector separately as the eigen decomposition calculation will have to be performed twice. Ideally, I'd like a "set_all_mass_properties" function exposed to GDScript in which I can enter the mass, center of mass, and full inertia in one step to eliminate redundant calculations. It would probably be enough to just have a "set_full_inertia" function, but setting the inertia and center of mass separately will still result in redundant calls to `_update_transform_dependent`. How do people feel about adding such functions?
3. Does anyone have any strong opinions on where the  `eigen_value_symmetric` function belongs? Should it remain in its own header file, or be moved to math_funcs. 

Finally, I recently happened across issue #80703.  This is something I hope to address in a future pull request once I'm finished with this one, but it's something I wanted to bring to people's attention. Should we chose to properly implement Euler's rigid body equations (something I will very much push for) I believe there's performance that could be gained by not computing the principle axes of inertia at all and instead only relying on the local inertia tensor. The entire scope of work would have to be identified, but I understand this would not be a trivial change. However, this pull request would lay the groundwork for that effort.

Note these are my personal opinions, I'm not a maintainer of godot (I'm the maintainer of Jolt Physics).

> I chose to use the "alternate" convention for expressing the products of inertia

Until you created this PR I had never seen anyone use the 'products of inertia' notation. I've always stored inertia as a rotation + diagonal or just plain as a tensor. Specifying the components of the inertia tensor directly is probably not understandable for most people, so if we use the 'normal' or 'alternate' version doesn't seem like a big deal to me. If we want a more user friendly version then I would suggest allowing the user to specify a rotation instead + a way of visualizing the resulting inertia tensor (but I can imagine that would complicate things in your sim).

> I'd like a "set_all_mass_properties" function exposed to GDScript in which I can enter the mass, center of mass, and full inertia in one step to eliminate redundant calculations.

Sounds like a good function to have to me.

> Does anyone have any strong opinions on where the eigen_value_symmetric function belongs?

No opinion.

> Finally, I recently happened across issue https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/80703. This is something I hope to address in a future pull request once I'm finished with this one, but it's something I wanted to bring to people's attention.

Added a reply there.

> Until you created this PR I had never seen anyone use the 'products of inertia' notation. I've always stored inertia as a rotation + diagonal or just plain as a tensor. 

Separating the inertia entries into two separate 3-element vectors wouldn't have been my ideal implementation if I were designing this from the ground-up. It's the best implementation I could conceive of while keeping the existing structure in place to maintain compatibility with existing projects. I didn't want to expose the raw tensor because I didn't want uninitiated users to treat it like a basis and enter a non-symmetrical matrix. This implementation means it can be safely ignored by the majority of users who don't care, while providing a decent interface for those who do. The choice of using Voigt notation was driven simply by having to choose how to order these elements and I turned to an already-established convention. To my knowledge, Voigt notation is never actually used in dynamics to represent inertia; it's something structural engineers would use to represent stress and strain tensors, which are similarly symmetric, but benefit from the 1-dimensional representation in actual calculation. 

> Specifying the components of the inertia tensor directly is probably not understandable for most people, so if we use the 'normal' or 'alternate' version doesn't seem like a big deal to me. If we want a more user friendly version then I would suggest allowing the user to specify a rotation instead + a way of visualizing the resulting inertia tensor (but I can imagine that would complicate things in your sim).

While I think you're right that there is some intuition behind exposing it as principle inertia and a principle basis (or rotation), in practice this actually complicates things. The way the inertia is actually computed in most cases is in a coordinate system that's already known (ie, the body-attached, or "local' frame). The Inertia tensor is built up from a variety of known masses within that coordinate system plus their individual inertias (if not modeled as point masses). As an example, here's how I model a simple fuel burn in GDScript using the additions from this pull request: 

```
extends RigidBody3D

var fuel = 20;  # kg
var fuel_loc : Vector3 = Vector3(0.5,0.5,0.0)
var mass_empty : float = 20.0;
var cg_empty : Vector3 = Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
var inertia_empty : Vector3 = mass_empty*Vector3(1.0,1.0,1.0)/12
var product_of_inertia_empty : Vector3 = Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)

var fuel_burn_rate : float = 1  # kg/s

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	
	var mass_tot : float = fuel+mass_empty
	var cg : Vector3 = (mass_empty*cg_empty + fuel*fuel_loc)/(mass_tot)
	
	var fuel_loc_from_cg : Vector3 = fuel_loc - cg
	
	# Calculate inertia for current fuel (assume fuel is a point mass)
	var inertia_tot : Vector3 = inertia_empty
	inertia_tot.x += fuel * (fuel_loc_from_cg.y**2 + fuel_loc_from_cg.z**2)
	inertia_tot.y += fuel * (fuel_loc_from_cg.x**2 + fuel_loc_from_cg.z**2)
	inertia_tot.z += fuel * (fuel_loc_from_cg.x**2 + fuel_loc_from_cg.y**2)
	
	var product_of_inertia_tot : Vector3 = product_of_inertia_empty
	product_of_inertia_tot.x += fuel * (fuel_loc_from_cg.y * fuel_loc_from_cg.z)
	product_of_inertia_tot.y += fuel * (fuel_loc_from_cg.x * fuel_loc_from_cg.z)
	product_of_inertia_tot.z += fuel * (fuel_loc_from_cg.x * fuel_loc_from_cg.y)
	
	# set mass properties (this is where a set_mass_properties function would be useful)
	set_mass(mass_tot)
	set_center_of_mass(cg)
	set_inertia(inertia_tot)
	set_product_of_inertia(product_of_inertia_tot)
	
	# burn fuel
	fuel -= fuel_burn_rate*delta;
	fuel = maxf(fuel, 0.0)
```

As you can see, this is actually quite easy to do. It also supports my choice of Voigt order because there's some nice consistency in the expressions (The x term in both vectors is dependent on the y and z coordinates of the mass, y on x and z, and z on x and y). And not having to remember to stick a negative sign in there is helpful as well, which supports the chosen sign convention, so I think I'm sticking with it (just got to make sure that's well documented). 

> Added a reply there.

While this is probably not the right place to discuss this, I think having a project setting to enable full calculation of the rotational dynamics is a good idea. I replied in the issue as well, and it can be discussed in the next pull request. 

I appreciate the feedback!
Finally got everything to check out. I believe this is now ready for review.
Is there a demo project I can use to test this? I'm not sure exactly how it should be configured.

I have attached a [simple project](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23515051/inertia-test.zip) with 2 cubes that experience an applied torque for 1 second after the game starts. The cube on the left has moments of inertia of 10kg*m^2 on all axes, The cube on the left has the same moments of inertia, but also has non-zero products of inertia. You'll see it rotates oddly. You can adjust the `products_of_inertia` field of the Mass Distribution section under RigidBody3D. In practice, this probably isn't something the user will be adjusting here; rather it would probably be computed within some script (see the cg_test.gd script for an example on how this might happen). 

You can optionally print out the Euler angles of one of the cubes by checking the `print_rotation` option I added. 

The actual rotation of the cube is not currently physically accurate and thus behaves very oddly; I will be following up with another PR to correct this motion and directly address #80703 (I already have it working on another branch).
